title: Summer flight chaos: what US travelers can actually claim in July and August
summary: The US has no EC 261-style payout — but some summer delays still qualify for $250-$650. Here's when, and the loophole most Americans miss.
body_markdown:
It's the last week of July, and the departures board at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta shows delay after delay — 79 cancellations and nearly 3,000 delays hit the US network in a single day, with the worst of it built through the afternoon at hubs from Atlanta to New York. Most travelers caught in that mess assume there's nothing to do but rebook. For a purely domestic trip, that's mostly true. But book a "Delta" flight home from Paris or Amsterdam this summer, and there's a real chance the plane you board isn't Delta's at all — and that detail alone can be worth up to $650.


If any part of that sounds familiar, here's the useful part: not every summer delay pays out, but plenty do — and knowing which is which takes about two minutes.


## What you're owed, at a glance


Distance


Compensation


Under 1,500 km (EU-linked flights only)


$270


1,500 km – 3,500 km (EU-linked flights only)


$430


Over 3,500 km (EU-linked flights only)


$650


Applies to delays of 3+ hours on arrival, cancellations with less than 14 days' notice, and denied boarding — under DOT rules (domestic) / EC 261 (EU-linked flights) — as long as the airline, not extraordinary circumstances, is responsible.


## Why is summer worse than any other season?


Domestic disruption in the US this summer has been driven by the same pressures as everywhere else — volume, weather, a certain global sports event, and network strain — rather than any single cause. On 26 June 2026, weather and air traffic control limits produced 2,615 delays and at least 75 cancellations by mid-evening, with the worst congestion at Chicago O'Hare, Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta, San Francisco, Harry Reid, Boston Logan and Miami. A month later, on 27 July, the pattern repeated: nearly 3,000 delays and 79 cancellations, again concentrated at the busiest domestic hubs. Neither event involved a European leg, which matters more than it might seem — because whether a delay is compensable in cash depends entirely on whether any part of the itinerary touches Europe.


For live tracking of disruption events like the ones below, see the[EU and US summer disruption hub.](https://www.airhelp.com/en/flight-disruptions/)


## What blocks a claim, and what doesn’t?


-


**Usually blocks a claim (extraordinary circumstances):** Weather and air traffic control restrictions (domestic and EU-linked flights alike); Security risks and political instability.


-


**Usually does NOT block a claim:** Under DOT rules: nothing removes your refund right if you decline to travel — refunds apply regardless of cause; Under EC 261 (EU-linked flights): technical/mechanical faults, crew scheduling, and airline staff strikes are NOT extraordinary circumstances and remain compensable.


For the full breakdown, see our[extraordinary circumstances explained.](https://www.airhelp.com/en/flight-rights-usa/)


### Real example: two disruptions, one summer, two different outcomes


#### US domestic network, 26 June 2026 — weather and ATC congestion


Thunderstorms and air traffic control flow restrictions produced 2,615 delays and at least 75 cancellations by mid-evening, with the worst congestion at Chicago O'Hare, Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta, San Francisco, Harry Reid, Boston Logan, and Miami, and knock-on problems reaching New York, Detroit, Minneapolis, Columbus and Washington.


**Verdict:** Purely domestic US flights aren't covered by EC 261 no matter the cause, so a cash payout doesn't apply here regardless of whether weather or the airline was at fault. What you're owed instead: an automatic refund if you decline to travel, plus rebooking, meals, or a hotel if the delay was within the airline's control per its published customer service plan.


Full details:[US flight disruption tracker (26 June)](https://www.airhelp.com/en/flight-disruptions/us-flight-disruptions-major-hubs-2690-delays-cancellations-26062026/)


#### The joint-venture loophole: when a "Delta" flight isn't Delta's


Delta runs a transatlantic joint venture with Air France, KLM and Virgin Atlantic, and sells tickets under its own flight numbers for legs those partners actually fly. A New York-to-Paris ticket sold as a Delta flight number, but operated by Air France aircraft and crew, is covered by EC 261 on the inbound leg — Air France is the operating carrier, and EC 261 follows the airline in the cockpit, not the name on the ticket.


**Verdict** : A 5-hour technical delay on that Paris-to-Atlanta route, for example, is worth $650 per passenger, exactly as if you'd booked Air France directly. Fly the same route on Delta's own aircraft instead, and there's no EC 261 claim — only the DOT refund rule applies.


Full details:[American Airlines compensation guide (operating-carrier rules)](https://www.airhelp.com/en/airlines/american-airlines/)


Equally, if you were flying out of the EU and back to the US after a European summer vacation, and your flight (on any airline) was significantly delayed, canceled, or overbooked, you’d be eligible for up to $650 compensation.


## Step-by-step: what to do at the airport


1.


Check the operating carrier for each leg of your trip, not just the airline name on your itinerary — this decides whether EC 261 is even in play.


2.


Ask a gate agent or check the airline's app for the specific reason for the delay — this matters for both DOT and EC 261 purposes.


3.


Hold onto your boarding pass, any rebooking confirmations, and receipts for anything you pay for yourself.


4.


If any leg departs the EU, or lands in the US after departing the EU on a European airline, check it separately for an EC 261 claim — nationality and residency don't matter.


5.


If you decide not to travel after a domestic 3+ hour delay (or international 6+ hour delay), you're entitled to an automatic refund, not a voucher.


6.


Keep every receipt if a delay costs you money out of pocket — reimbursement policies vary by airline's customer service commitments.


7.


[Submit your claim with AirHelp!](https://funnel.airhelp.com/claims/new?lang=en)

## FAQ


#### Is there a US law like the EU's for flight delay compensation?


No. The US Department of Transportation guarantees a refund if you decline to travel and denied-boarding compensation up to $2,150, but there's no federal law requiring airlines to pay cash just for a long delay or cancellation.


#### How can a Delta flight be covered by EU rules?


Delta's transatlantic joint venture with Air France, KLM and Virgin Atlantic means some "Delta" flight numbers are actually operated by those partner airlines. EC 261 follows the operating carrier, so if a European partner is flying the plane, EC 261 can apply even though you booked with an American carrier.


#### What's the fastest way to check if my flight qualifies?


Check each leg of your trip separately: confirm the operating airline (not just the marketing name on your ticket) and the departure and arrival airports, then run it through a free eligibility check.


#### Does a strike ever qualify for compensation?


On EU-linked flights, it depends who's striking — airline staff strikes are compensable, third-party strikes (ground handlers, ATC) usually aren't. On US domestic flights, there's no compensation either way, only refund and care rights.
